title: The Channel Tunnel: earlier attempts, how it was bored from both coasts, and the 1990 breakthrough

sources.title: Europe: An Island No More. Hello! Allo!
sources.note: 1990 年 11 月的報導：10 月 30 日英方鑽出的探測孔打通、兩端水平偏差約 20 英寸、預告 12 月 1 日雙方握手

sources.title: The Channel gets its tunnel, 25 years ago
A Railway Under the Ocean: The Channel Tunnel Linking Britain and France

facts.text: In 1802, a French engineer presented Napoleon Bonaparte with a plan for a tunnel under the Channel.
Digging began in the late 19th century (1878 to 1883) and again in the 1970s (1973 to 1975), but both attempts were abandoned.
Boring of the tunnel that was finally built took place between January 1988 and June 1991.
Eleven tunnel boring machines were used: six started from the British side and five from the French side.
The tunnels were bored through a chalk layer, chalk marl, that is solid, unlikely to fracture, and resistant to groundwater because it contains clay.
The service tunnel between the two railway tunnels was dug ahead of them to probe and confirm the rock conditions.
On 30 October 1990, a thin probe drilled from the British side broke through the last rock of the service tunnel.
Measurements showed the two approaches were out of line horizontally by only about 20 inches, roughly half a meter.
On 1 December 1990, workers from the two sides broke through the final wall of rock in the service tunnel and shook hands.
The link meant that Britain was joined to the European mainland for the first time since the last Ice Age.
The tunnel opened on 6 May 1994; it has two railway tunnels and a service tunnel, each about 50 km long, 37 km of them under the sea.
